profile.summary: These are the two labelled sets Brandes et al. built to test whether a protein language model can score coding variants that are not single amino acid substitutions. One holds 3,470 in-frame insertions, deletions and deletion-insertion combinations from ClinVar, 1,791 pathogenic and 1,679 benign; the other holds 36,000 or so ClinVar stop-gain variants, split by whether the new stop codon is expected to trigger nonsense-mediated decay. Both are scored by ROC-AUC for separating pathogenic from benign. They are useful to anyone asking whether a sequence model's likelihood scores transfer from missense variants to indels and truncations.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether an effect score separates pathogenic from benign variants in two classes of coding variant that most variant effect predictors cannot handle: in-frame indels, which change the length of the protein, and stop gains, which truncate it. The authors' point is that a protein language model can be applied to any amino acid sequence, so it can score these as well as missense variants. The stop-gain set is further split by nonsense-mediated decay, because a truncation often acts at the transcript level rather than through the protein sequence a language model sees.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, ESM1b can predict the effects of multiresidue variants

quotes.text: Unlike most VEP methods, protein language models can assess any amino acid sequence and, therefore, be leveraged to predict the effects of any coding mutation, including in-frame indels and stop gains.
We use the term ‘indels’ to include insertions, deletions and deletion–insertion (delins) combinations.
ESM1b is a protein language model trained to assess protein sequence variations, while the effects of stop-gains are often at the transcript level through nonsense-mediated decay (NMD)

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Both sets are drawn from ClinVar, with labels downloaded from the ClinVar variant_summary table, and the authors say only high-confidence variants were included, with the processing described in the Supplementary Methods. The published indel table holds 3,470 rows against RefSeq NM transcripts, each with the wild-type and mutated sequence, the affected window, the number of amino acids affected and the length difference, labelled 1 for 1,791 variants and 0 for 1,679; its mut_type column gives 2,248 deletions, 937 insertions and 285 delins. The stop-gain set is partitioned with the 50 base pair rule, which treats a transcript as likely to undergo decay only if the new stop codon falls more than 50 bases upstream of the last exon junction in the coding region, applied using exon annotations from the human genome.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A method supplies one score per variant and the whole set is treated as a single classification task, scored by global ROC-AUC rather than averaged per gene; the authors argue a global figure is more informative for clinical use because variants are compared across genes. For indels the model score is the pseudo-log-likelihood ratio between the mutated and wild-type sequences, in three variants: plain, weighted by sequence length, and absolute valued. For stop gains the score is the lowest log-likelihood ratio among all possible missense variants in the region lost after the new stop codon. Differences between methods are tested by a permutation test over 2,000 iterations, shuffling the scores between variants, with one-tailed empirical p values and a floor of p below 0.001. Uncertainty on the stop-gain figures comes from bootstrapping 140 pathogenic and 140 benign variants from each group over 20 iterations.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Generalized effect scores for indels and stop-gain variants, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification, Testing for significant performance differences

We refer to the PLLR score described above as ‘vanilla’ PLLR, while also considering the following two minor variations: (1) weighted PLLR and (2) absolute-valued PLLR
defined as the LLR score assigned to the missense variant predicted to be the most deleterious among all possible missense variants in the lost region of the protein

We treated the entire set of pathogenic and benign variants (from ClinVar<sup><xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10">10</xref></sup> or HGMD/gnomAD<sup><xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9">9</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR26">26</xref></sup>) as a single genome-wide classification task to calculate a global ROC-AUC.

The empirical one-tailed <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> value was the fraction of 2,000 iterations where the difference in output metric was as extreme as that with the actual, nonpermuted effect scores.
In each bootstrapping iteration, we randomly sampled 140 pathogenic and 140 benign variants from each of the three groups of stop-gain variants

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: On the indel set the absolute-valued score reaches ROC-AUC 0.874, ahead of the plain 0.869 and the weighted 0.861, and all three beat CADD at 0.835; on delins variants alone the gap is wider, 0.887 against 0.671. The three sequence-similarity baselines are near or below 0.6: edit distance 0.501, pairwise alignment 0.586, BlastP 0.581. On stop gains, ESM1b scores 0.734 on variants not expected to undergo decay but only 0.565 on those that are, and on the non-decay group it beats the number of residues lost (0.649) and the fraction of the protein lost (0.599). The authors also estimate from the score distribution that 52% of in-frame indel variants of uncertain significance in ClinVar are pathogenic.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository publishes both benchmark tables with every method's scores already in them, so a comparison can be reproduced from the files alone. To score new variants, install the listed dependencies and run the multi-residue scoring script, which takes a CSV of wild-type sequence, mutated sequence and start position; a separate script scores all possible missense substitutions in a FASTA file, which is the route used for stop gains.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train, validation or test split: each set is evaluated whole as a single classification task, which the authors can do because the method is unsupervised. The only partitioning is by variant class for reporting: deletions, insertions and delins for the indel set, and the 50 base pair decay rule for the stop-gain set.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Global ROC-AUC on pathogenic versus benign, higher better, computed over the whole set rather than averaged per gene. Elsewhere in the paper a label-balanced PRC-AUC is also used, obtained by downsampling each class to 80% of the minority class 100 times and averaging, but the indel and stop-gain figures are reported as ROC-AUC.

quotes.text: we primarily used ROC-AUC (Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2b,e–h</xref>), the standard evaluation metric for binary classifiers<sup><xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR61">61
we randomly downsampled each dataset into an equal number of pathogenic and benign variants (80% of the variants in the minority class) and calculated the PRC-AUC over the balanced dataset
The absolute-value PLLR marginally outperforms (ROC-AUC = 0.874) the vanilla (0.869) and weighted PLLR (0.861).

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: On indels, one published predictor and three simple scores: CADD, plus Levenshtein edit distance, a pairwise alignment score (match 2, mismatch minus 1) and BlastP with BLOSUM62 and gap penalties. On stop gains, no published predictor at all, and three simple scores: number of residues lost, percentage of residues lost, and the binary 50 base pair rule. The authors state why: nearly all indel and stop-gain predictors are trained on clinical databases, which would make evaluation on ClinVar circular, and CADD is the exception they could use.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects

quotes.text: The vast majority of these have been trained on clinical databases like ClinVar, leading to circularity issues when evaluating them on the same benchmarks. Therefore, we compared ESM1b to only one other VEP method (CADD) over the ClinVar benchmark of in-frame indels (Fig. <xref rid="Fig6" ref-type="fig">6b</xref>) and none over stop-gain variants (Fig. <xref rid="Fig6" ref-type="fig">6d</xref>).
For in-frame indels, we considered baseline scores based on the followings: (1) edit distance, (2) pairwise alignment and (3) BlastP.
For stop-gain variants, we considered the following baseline scores: (1) the number of residues lost, (2) the percentage of residues lost (relative to the WT sequence length) and (3) the 50 bp rule.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The main control is the choice of comparators, not a data split. Because the evaluated method is unsupervised, the authors argue there is no leakage from training into these ClinVar sets, and they exclude predictors trained on clinical databases to avoid circularity, which is why only CADD appears on indels and nothing on stop gains. The sets themselves are restricted to high-confidence ClinVar variants. No sequence identity cut-off between the indel set and anything else is described.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Bootstrapped standard deviations on the stop-gain figures and permutation p values on the indel comparison. For Fig. 6d, 140 pathogenic and 140 benign variants were sampled from each group over 20 iterations, and the error bars are the standard deviation of the resulting ROC-AUCs. For Fig. 6b, one-tailed p values from 2,000 permutations are reported for the difference between CADD and each ESM1b score, with p below 0.001 when no permutation matched the observed gap. facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Protein sequence for the evaluated method: the wild-type and mutated amino acid sequences, with no alignment or structure. Where a sequence exceeds the model's 1,022 amino acid limit, the score is computed on a window containing the affected region with 511 residues of context before it and enough after to fill the limit. The stop-gain score needs the position of the new stop codon, and the 50 base pair rule needs exon annotations, which is transcript-level information used for the partition rather than by the model.

quotes.text: Given the protein length limit of ESM1b, if either the WT or mutated sequences exceed 1,022 amino acids, PLLR is calculated using subsequences that satisfy this constraint.
Before the indel, we include a segment of 511 residues (or as many as there are).
`wt_seq`: the wild type (original) protein sequence
`start_pos`: the starting position (1-indexed) of the mutation relative to the wild type sequence

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot. The scores are likelihood ratios from a pretrained protein language model with no fitting to these labels; the only choices are which of the three pseudo-log-likelihood ratio forms to use for indels, and taking the minimum missense score over the lost region for stop gains. CADD, the one published comparator, is a supervised method.

run_guide.summary: Get the published benchmark tables, and score new multi-residue variants with the repository's command-line tool.
prerequisites: Python with tqdm, numpy, pandas, biopython, torch and fair-esm, as the README's install line lists.
The ESM1b weights, which fair-esm downloads; the README notes the model comes from Meta AI's official repository.
For scoring a new set, a CSV with wt_seq, mut_seq and start_pos columns.
The code is MIT licensed. ClinVar labels are public; the HGMD part of the wider paper is not, but neither of these two benchmarks uses it.

No published command computes the reported ROC-AUCs, the permutation tests or the bootstrapped error bars; the repository publishes the scored tables and the scoring tools only.

The stop-gain pipeline is not a single command: the minimisation over missense scores in the lost region and the 50 base pair partition are described in the paper, not shipped as a script in the files read.

notes: Written from the PMC full text (PMC10484790, CC BY 4.0) and two files of ntranoslab/esm-variants (MIT) at commit 0c33758a5073e5d6e673d9a16a40e5b0af46851d. Points for a human. First, the stop-gain counts disagree between the Fig. 6d legend (32,362 and 36,034 pathogenic) and the Methods bootstrapping description (32,441 and 36,113); the legend figures are used here and the sizes in the three stop-gain entries are the legend's pathogenic plus benign sums, so they should be checked against the published stop-gain file before being quoted anywhere. Second, the indel entry's size was verified against the published table: 3470 rows, 1791 with label 1, 1679 with label 0, and mut_type counts of 2248 deletions, 937 insertions and 285 delins. Third, data_licence is null because no licence is stated for ClinVar-derived labels in the sources read. Fourth, the ROC-AUC values appear on the figures and in the prose; Supplementary Table 2 holds the full evaluations and was not read. Fifth, the saved indel benchmark CSV is about 15 MB, which the applier may not want in the repository even though its licence allows it.
